title: Chiral Tubular Magnonic Crystals with Periodic Dzyaloshinskii--Moriya Interaction
authors: P. Contreras-Gallardo, J. Flores-Farias, B. Mimica-Figari, V. Puliafito, P. Landeros, R. A. Gallardo
abstract: We introduce a chiral tubular magnonic crystal formed by a ferromagnetic nanotube with a periodically modulated interfacial Dzyaloshinskii--Moriya interaction (DMI). Using a plane-wave formalism adapted to the cylindrical geometry, we calculate the spin-wave band structure including exchange, nonlocal dipolar coupling, and interfacial DMI. We show that the tubular geometry qualitatively modifies the role of periodic DMI compared with planar chiral magnonic crystals. Besides producing the usual nonreciprocal frequency shift, curvature converts part of the interfacial DMI into an effective anisotropy-like internal field. This creates a sign-dependent frequency landscape along the tube, so that DMI-covered regions can act either as potential wells or barriers for the lowest-frequency modes. As a result, flat and weakly dispersive bands appear in both Damon--Eshbach-like and backward-volume-like configurations, with the latter having no direct counterpart in planar systems. Our results identify periodically engineered DMI in nanotubes as a route for controlling nonreciprocal spin waves, localized modes, and flat magnonic bands in curved architectures.
summary: This work theoretically analyzes spin waves in a chiral nanotube where the Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction is periodically modulated. By adapting plane-wave methods to cylindrical geometry, the authors show that the tube curvature fundamentally changes how the DMI acts. This engineering capability allows for the creation of flat, non-dispersive magnon bands, offering a route to control spin wave behavior in curved magnetic architectures.
main_problem: The study investigates how a periodically modulated interfacial Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction (DMI) alters the spin-wave band structure within a chiral tubular magnonic crystal.
main_result: The tubular geometry modifies the DMI's role by converting part of it into an effective anisotropy field, leading to flat, weakly dispersive bands in both Damon–Eshbach-like and backward-volume-like configurations.
method: The analysis employs a plane-wave formalism adapted for cylindrical geometry to solve the spin-wave eigenvalue problem derived from the Landau–Lifshitz equation.
model_or_system: The system is a ferromagnetic nanotube patterned with heavy-metal rings to induce a periodic DMI. The dynamics are governed by the LL equation, incorporating exchange, dipolar, and DMI couplings.
key_observables: Spin-wave band structure, nonreciprocal frequency shift, and the appearance of flat/weakly dispersive bands.
important_parameters: DMI constant (D), tube curvature, and the angle ($	heta$) defining the equilibrium magnetization state.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes small-amplitude spin-wave deviations and neglects concomitant modulations of other magnetic parameters.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically shows the setup: a nanotube with periodic DMI modulation. Figure 2 displays the spin-wave band structures for different DMI strengths in DE and BV configurations. Figure 3 compares spatial profiles of the lowest-frequency eigenmodes in nanotubes versus planar films.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical model (nanotube with periodic DMI), details the theoretical framework (plane-wave formalism on cylindrical geometry), presents the key findings regarding the modification of the band structure by curvature, and concludes by identifying this engineered DMI as a control mechanism for spin waves.
why_interesting: The findings on flat bands and non-reciprocity in curved geometries provide novel platforms for controlling spin wave dynamics, which is relevant to understanding energy band engineering in magnetic systems.
